The Ultimate Guide to Claude Design for Product Teams
Idea to prototype in hours. Design to shipped code in days. Five gaps still bite. Tested on real production code, not a demo.
I pointed Claude Design at accredia[.]io's GitHub repo and asked it to build admin onboarding for a new organization.
10 minutes later I had a fully interactive prototype I could iterate on.
Not a mockup. Not a screenshot. A clickable flow built on top of my real design system, ready to share, comment, refine, and implement.
Example: accredia[.]io. prototype with Claude Design
Some compare Claude Design to Figma speed on the canvas. Wrong unit.
What matters for a product team is Time to Learn - the time from "we should try X" to "we have evidence it works or fails." Claude Design can radically reduce it.

1. What changes for your team

Claude Design compresses two parts of the workflow.
Idea → prototype:
  • Old: several days with a dedicated designer. Weeks if you don't have capacity.
  • New: same afternoon. Iterate in hours via chat, comments, or sketch.
Approved design → code in production:
  • Old: weeks. You hand Figma to engineers. Engineers rebuild in code. Implementation drifts. Back-and-forth on what the design "really" meant.
  • New: days. Engineers continue from the prototype and design system through Claude Code. No rebuild.
Some say Figma is faster for experienced designers. The gap is smaller than these two compressions. And it shrinks further when you pick the right model. Sonnet for small fixes.
Designers should adopt this too. Cleaner handoff to engineering. More time on the work that needs design judgment instead of checking pixels.
The same design system also generates slide decks, motion videos, and custom templates. Marketing, sales, and support reuse the brand without rebuilding it.

2. How to define your design system

Most product teams have a design system in some form. A Figma library, a Storybook, a brand doc. Start by importing what you have.
STEP 1: Open Claude Design > Design systems > Create
Go to
https://claude.ai/design
.
STEP 2: Provide company name, examples, and sources
You can mix multiple sources and also drop in sketches, screenshots, photos, fonts, logos, and a text description of voice and brand. Claude Design can also pull context from the open web.
I tested reverse-engineering my existing codebase. According to multiple user reports, code wins when both code and Figma exist.
Note: DESIGN.md (introduced by Google) is the lowest-fidelity option in the table because it's rules-only. No assets, no components, no motion, and not all layout patterns. It's a fast seed when you have nothing. Move to a codebase or .fig file as soon as you have one.
Tip: For a new product without a system yet, you can clone an existing brand you admire (Ferrari, Apple, Linear) and iterate from there. Faster than starting from a moodboard, and you keep refining until it's yours.
You can also run multiple design systems in parallel. Useful if you ship across product lines, or if you're testing a brand refresh without breaking production.
STEP 3: Click "Continue to generation"
Three artifacts:
  • Design System. UI kit, type, colors, spacing, components, brand. Every prototype anchors on this.
  • Design Files. Assets, HTML, images, stylesheets you can preview.
  • Skill.md. A skill Claude Design generates as a representation of the design system. The agent uses it to keep every new design consistent with your brand.
You can review your design system, iterate via chat, set permissions, and share with the team. Comments work the same way they do in Figma.
Step 4: (Optional) Export your design system as a skill
When you export your design system as a .zip archive, it becomes a skill you can give to any agent (Claude Code, Cowork, Codex). The skill is a complete representation of the system and contains all design files.
That's the theory. In my tests, I faced errors. Waiting for a fix.

3. How to prototype a product or feature

Same flow whether you're prototyping something new or modifying what already ships. The difference is what you point Claude Design at on the way in.
STEP 1: Open Claude Design > New prototype > Create
Pick the design system you generated in §2 and name your prototype.
STEP 2: Provide context
Depending on what you're prototyping:
  • New feature. Brief Claude Design from scratch.
  • Existing feature. Point at the codebase, or branch from a previous Claude Design version.
You can also include screenshots, Figma files, web elements, or reference Claude Design projects (via "Import").
What to brief it on:
  • Objective. Why it's important and how success will be measured. Often implicit when you have a well-documented system.
  • Persona. Who's actually using this. Not the buyer. The person inside the screen.
  • Value proposition. What this screen is supposed to deliver to that person.
  • Job to be done. The underlying task they're trying to complete.
  • Common actions. What they'll do most often. If you have product analytics, lead with those numbers. If not, your best assumptions.
There is no GitHub repo selector, but after connecting GitHub you can provide Claude Design with a GitHub URL. I specified a GitHub repo for a new feature because my agents maintain a full strategic context in the repo.
This isn't just prompt engineering. It's instrumenting business context for the agent beyond the current objective, just like we discussed in the newsletter (Opus 4.7, Intent Engineering Framework).
STEP 3: Answer the questions > Continue
If you forgot about the context, don't worry. Claude Design interviews you before taking action.
STEP 4: Review and refine in the canvas
5–10 minutes for the first generation. Once the prototype exists, switch to a faster model in chat. Iteration drops to seconds. An example result:
PMs can run small fixes like copy edits, button placement, or empty-state polish without pulling in a designer for every adjustment.
Four refinement tools:
  • Chat. Refine via natural language ("make the empty state more inviting").
  • Comments. Figma-style threaded notes. Anyone you share it with can drop them.
  • Sketch. Draw directly on the prototype. Useful when "move that there" is faster than typing.
  • Edit. Apply changes directly in the system. I use it primarily for text adjustments:
Edit: Apply changes directly in the system
Each prototype can have multiple variants on the same canvas. They're called tweaks. Just ask in the Chat. Claude Design adds them to the Tweaks panel. For example, here I asked for an Anthropic variant:
STEP 5: Export and hand off
Six export options: PDF, PPTX, ZIP, Standalone HTML, Canva, Claude Code handoff.
The Claude Code handoff is what changes the workflow the most. Your prototype isn't a deliverable engineers re-implement. It's a starting point they continue from.

4. What doesn't work yet (it's a research preview)

Five gaps after a week of real use.
Integration with the rest of the stack
  • No MCP support. Claude Design doesn't connect to MCP servers and doesn't expose an MCP server yet. GrowthBook has a public MCP server. Linear has one. So does most of your stack. This is the single biggest gap.
  • No backlog or issue tracker sync. Half your work comes out of Claude Design (new features, modifications). The other half comes out of Jira or Linear (bugs, internal tools, infrastructure). My take: stay on Jira or Linear for tickets, treat Claude Design projects as the place where the design lives, and link prototypes manually until sync ships.
Workflow surface area
  • No status, previews, or filters on designs. Engineering can't tell which Claude Design projects are ready to pull versus still under iteration. A status field plus filters (ready / in review / shipped) would make the handoff much cleaner. Jira / Linear statuses can fill that gap:
  • No built-in experiment runner. You can export Figma prototypes to Maze and run usability tests at scale. With Claude Design you'll rely on external tools and manual exports until more integrations appear. Compensated by shipping faster and learning from real usage.
Where additional context lives
  • No clear home for supporting notes. Where do test cases, customer interview notes, and extra reference files for a specific design go? Comments handle quick feedback in the moment. But there's no place for supporting notes you want to keep tied to a design over time.
For each gap, the workaround is the same. Stay on Jira or Linear for tickets. Use Claude Design for design. Run experiments in your existing stack or ship earlier and learn in production.
The gaps will close. The compression won't reverse.
